reason: I want to build the pump, and heart muscle should provide the force its chambers need.
expectation: The heart muscle will fit into the pumping walls slot, making the chambers able to contract; they may still need valves and a rhythm.

alternatives.reason: Valves also fit the pump goal, but I chose to add the pumping walls first.

effect: The muscle now forms contracting chamber walls, so I’ll add the valves to continue assembling the pump.
reaction: The thickening outlines make the muscle’s role clear, though the fitting was expected.
reason: Valves should control the direction of blood flow through the chambers.
expectation: The valves will fill the direction-control slot; the pump may still need pacemaker cells for rhythm.

alternatives.reason: The vessel network also serves a goal, but I want to finish the chamber fittings first.

effect: The valves are fitted and their arrows show how they prevent reverse flow. The pacemaker cells are now available to complete the pump's rhythm.
reaction: The forward and reverse arrows make the valves' purpose clear; the result was expected.
reason: The pacemaker cells should provide the rhythm needed for the pump.
expectation: The cells will add a spreading electrical rhythm to the fitted heart chambers, completing the pump or bringing it closer to completion.

alternatives.reason: The vessel network also advances a goal, but I want to finish assembling the pump first.

effect: The pacemaker completed the beating heart, and the result clarifies that the heart starts its own beat while nerves can adjust it. I’ll now build the exchange route.
reaction: The coordinated contraction was expected; the distinction between starting and adjusting the beat was useful.
reason: Connecting the vessels and capillaries seems like the next step toward a route that carries blood back to the heart.
expectation: The capillary networks will connect the arteries and veins into an exchange route, though it may still need to be linked to the heart.

alternatives.reason: Hemoglobin in red-cell envelopes should help carry oxygen, but I want to assemble the route first.

effect: The capillaries now connect outward and returning vessels, though the circuit has not yet been linked to the heart.
reaction: The arrows make the return route clear; the result was expected.
reason: This is the only offered combination, and it should make cells that carry oxygen.
expectation: Hemoglobin will go into the flexible red-cell envelopes to make oxygen-carrying red cells.

effect: The red blood cells contain hemoglobin and make ATP from sugar without nuclei or mitochondria. Combining them with plasma looks like the next step toward blood.
reaction: The lack of mitochondria was a useful contrast with the muscle cells.
reason: This is the only offered combination, and plasma should carry the red blood cells.
expectation: The red blood cells and plasma will form blood that can eventually circulate through the vessel circuit.

effect: The red blood cells and plasma formed oxygen-carrying blood, with sugar in the surrounding fluid. I can now put it into the vessel circuit.
reaction: The distinction between hemoglobin inside cells and sugar in plasma is clear; the result was expected.
reason: This is the only offered combination, and putting blood into the circuit should advance the delivery route.
expectation: The blood will fill the connected vessels, though the circuit may still need the heart to pump it.

effect: The blood-filled circuit shows exchange with tissue cells and completes the return-route goal; connecting the heart is now the next step.
reaction: The inset clearly shows that oxygen and nutrients leave the blood while red cells stay inside.
reason: This is the only offered combination, and the heart should pump blood through the circuit.
expectation: The beating heart will connect to the blood-filled circuit and put blood into circulation.

effect: The heart and blood-filled vessels now form a closed circulation, completing the chapter. The result connects the return route to transport throughout the body.
reaction: Seeing the parts form a complete loop was satisfying, though the result was expected.

mostWorthwhile.text: Filling the vessel circuit was most worthwhile because the tissue-exchange inset connected circulation to the oxygen and nutrients cells need, while showing that red blood cells stay inside the vessels.

leastWorthwhile.text: Combining plasma and red blood cells was clear but predictable, and it was one of several steps with only one offered combination.

surprise.text: I was interested that red blood cells lack mitochondria yet still make ATP from sugar in their fluid. That contrasted clearly with the muscle cells.

arbitrary.text: No action felt clearly arbitrary: each contributed to the pump, blood, or vessel route. Several later choices were compulsory, so they offered little room for a decision.

continue.text: I would probably continue to see how circulation connects to the rest of the body, though I would hope for more meaningful choices than the sequence of single options near the end.
